> I’m making a pocket-sized “radio” that tunes into fictional transmissions. Turning a dial changes the sounds and lights, while a hidden touch-sensitive spot unlocks a secret station. The PCB itself will look like a strange piece of recovered technology, with glowing cutouts and clues printed on the back.

## Design

### 2026-10-11 – ## Project idea

**5h**

## Project idea
I planned Signal Lost as a small interactive radio that tunes into fictional transmissions. The idea combines a tuning dial, mysterious sounds, and a hidden touch input that reveals a secret station.

## Schematic
I created the KiCad schematic around the QT Py ESP32-S3. I included connections for the rotary encoder, touch pad, indicator LEDs, and external audio amplifier.

## Custom symbols and footprints
I added custom KiCad library parts for the controller, rotary encoder, and touch pad. These give the PCB layout the mounting and connection details needed for the design.

### 2026-10-11 – ## PCB layout

**5h**

## PCB layout
I designed an 80 × 55 mm, two-layer carrier board and routed its connections. I also added clues to the back silkscreen to support the project’s mysterious radio theme.

## Controls and display
I wrote firmware for switching stations with the encoder and toggling playback with its push button. I added OLED station names and frequencies, blinking LEDs, and touch detection for the hidden “UNKNOWN” station.

## Audio
I programmed different synthesized sounds for Night Weather, Distress, Numbers, and Deep Space, plus the secret station. The sounds use tones, pulses, and static sent through I2S to the external amplifier.

### 2026-10-11 – Parts and assembly planning

**5h**

Parts and assembly planning
I put together a parts list and documented how the controller, OLED, amplifier, and speaker connect. This gives me a clear reference for assembling the prototype.

Verification
I documented the design checks: the schematic passed without errors or warnings, and the PCB had no errors or unconnected pads, with one silkscreen warning. The firmware compiled successfully; physical assembly and testing are still ahead.

Fabrication files
I exported Gerbers, drill files, schematic previews, and a complete design package. These collect the files needed for board fabrication and reviewing the prototype.
